The Torrent sucker (Thoburnia rhothoeca) is a small-bodied catostomid inhabiting fast-flowing headwater streams of the Appalachian region. Recent field surveys indicate that females reach sexual maturity at a total length of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters], with puberty typically occurring around three years of age based on scale annuli analysis. The weight of a female at this reproductive milestone averages 4.5 grams [Wwp = 4.5 grams], reflecting the modest body size characteristic of this species compared to many other suckers. The maximum recorded total length for the species is 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters], an ultimate size that places it among the more diminutive members of the Catostomidae family. Individuals attaining this length are rarely encountered, suggesting that considerable mortality occurs before the upper size limit is reached. The wet weight of a neonate upon emergence from the egg mass is estimated at 0.0031 grams [Wwb = 0.0031 grams], a value extrapolated from the relationship between egg diameter and mass observed in the closely related Erimyzon oblongus.

Body mass data collected from a series of preserved museum specimens reveals that the ultimate wet weight of Torrent sucker reaches approximately 38.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 38.3 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to the largest individuals captured. This asymptotic mass is consistent with the general pattern seen in other small-bodied catostomids inhabiting cool, well-oxygenated riffle habitats. Females at the onset of puberty, identified through histological examination of gonadal tissue, exhibit a wet weight near 4.5 grams [Wwp = 4.5 grams], a threshold that appears closely tied to the attainment of a corresponding total length of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters]. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a typical allometric trajectory, with the weight increasing roughly as the cube of length. These morphological parameters provide a baseline for assessing condition factors across different stream populations.

Life span estimates for the Torrent sucker are based on mark-recapture studies conducted in the Tygart Valley River system. The oldest individuals documented in the field were estimated at 7 years [am = 7 years] of age, a longevity record that was recorded at a mean annual water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This thermal regime, characteristic of the species' montane habitat, appears to constrain metabolic rates and thereby influence the pace of aging. The 2,555-day maximum lifespan (2,555 days) [am = 2,555 days] observed under these conditions is notably shorter than that reported for some congeneric suckers living in warmer lowland streams, where growth rates are higher but senescence may be accelerated at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The specific lifespan value was derived from recaptures of tagged individuals over a decade-long monitoring program, providing robust empirical support for this demographic parameter.

The reproductive ecology of Thoburnia rhothoeca is tied to spring spawning runs triggered by rising water temperatures. Females produce a single clutch of eggs annually [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs annually], with the number of oocytes per clutch ranging from 1,200 to 1,800 eggs [N_R_i = per clutch ranging from 1,200 to 1,800 eggs]. These fecundity estimates, obtained by dissecting gravid females collected during the spawning period, are relatively modest compared to other catostomids of similar size. The small egg diameter, averaging about 1.8 millimeters, yields a correspondingly modest neonatal wet weight of roughly 0.0031 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0031 grams], a value that underscores the altricial state of the newly hatched larvae. The adhesive demersal eggs are deposited in crevices among cobble substrate, where they incubate for several weeks before the yolk-sac larvae emerge.

Comparative physiological studies have examined the metabolic consequences of the species' cool-water habitat. The reproductive schedule appears finely tuned to the thermal regime, with female puberty, defined by the onset of vitellogenesis, occurring when individuals attain a total length of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters]. At this size, the corresponding body mass of approximately 4.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 4.5 grams] represents a significant energetic investment in somatic growth before the allocation of resources to gamete production. The ultimate total length of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters] for the species corresponds to an adult body mass of roughly 38.3 grams [Wwi = roughly 38.3 grams], a value that the longest-lived individuals, surviving up to 7 years [am = up to 7 years] under the prevailing 13 °C [T = 13 °C] stream temperatures, are able to approach. This life history strategy, characterized by slow growth and delayed reproduction relative to body size, is well suited to the stable but resource-limited environment of Appalachian headwater streams.
